title: Spring Lecture #6: Circular Dependency in Spring

questions.question: What does Spring's default `singleton` scope actually guarantee?
options: Only one object of that class can ever exist in the whole JVM
Only one object of that class can exist per thread
One shared object per bean definition inside the Spring container
One object per HTTP request handled by the application
questions.explanation: Spring singleton means the container keeps one shared instance per bean definition (bean name). It is not the classic Singleton design pattern: you can still `new` the class yourself, and two `@Bean` methods returning the same class give two singleton objects. One object per HTTP request is the `request` web scope.

questions.question: `OrderService` needs `PaymentService` in its constructor, and `PaymentService` needs `OrderService` in its constructor. Why can't Spring create these beans?
options: Constructor injection needs every argument before the object exists, so neither bean can be created first
Spring creates beans in alphabetical order and `OrderService` comes first
Two beans may never refer to each other's types in Spring
Constructor injection only works for classes annotated with `@Configuration`
questions.explanation: To call `new OrderService(...)` Spring needs a finished `PaymentService`, which itself needs a finished `OrderService` - there is no starting point, so startup fails (e.g. `BeanCurrentlyInCreationException`). Spring orders creation by dependencies, not alphabetically. The same loop in plain Java with `new` inside constructors ends in `StackOverflowError`.

questions.question: Each checkout needs its own `OrderRequest` object that stores that order's items and address, while `PaymentService` only contains reusable payment logic. Which scopes fit best?
options: Both singleton, because singleton is the default
`OrderRequest` singleton, `PaymentService` prototype
Both prototype, so nothing is ever shared
`OrderRequest` prototype (stateful), `PaymentService` singleton (stateless)
questions.explanation: The notes' rule: singleton for stateless beans that only provide behaviour, prototype for stateful beans holding changing data. A singleton `OrderRequest` would be shared by every checkout and mix their data, while making stateless services prototype just creates needless objects.

questions.explanation: There are two bean definitions, both singleton and eager, so two objects are created during startup and none on `getBean`. Asking for `getOrder` twice returns the same object (`true`), but `getOrder2` is a different bean definition with its own object (`false`) - singleton is per bean definition, not per class.

questions.explanation: The eager singleton `CheckoutService` needs a `Cart` in its constructor, so one prototype (id 1) is created first and stored; both `checkout()` calls reuse it. Prototype means a new object each time it is requested from the container, so the explicit `getBean(Cart.class)` creates cart 2. It does not mean a new object each time a singleton's method runs.

questions.question: You marked a slow `ReportService` with `@Component @Lazy` to speed up startup, but the log still shows it being constructed during startup. `DashboardService` (a normal `@Component`) takes `ReportService` as a constructor argument. What explains this?
options: The eager singleton `DashboardService` needs it, so Spring must create `ReportService` at startup to satisfy that dependency
`@Lazy` only works on prototype beans
`@Lazy` is ignored unless `@Scope("singleton")` is written explicitly
Component scanning always instantiates every class it finds
questions.explanation: A lazy bean is still created at startup when an eagerly created singleton directly depends on it, because that dependency must be satisfied. To really defer it, mark the injection point (`@Lazy ReportService` in the constructor) so a proxy is injected, or make the consumer lazy too. Scanning only registers bean definitions; it does not force creation of lazy beans.

questions.question: Why are singleton beans eagerly initialized by default, even though some may not be used right away?
options: Because eager creation uses less memory than lazy creation
Because lazy beans cannot have dependencies
Because prototype beans require all singletons to exist first
Because configuration or dependency errors then fail fast at startup instead of when the first user hits the feature
questions.explanation: Eager creation gives fast failure, early error detection and predictable startup validation. The trade-off of lazy initialization (including Boot's `spring.main.lazy-initialization=true`) is faster startup but errors that surface only when the bean is first used. Memory is not the reason - eager creation uses at least as much.

questions.question: This is the lecture's `BeanInitializationDemo`: the two services depend on each other through constructors. What happens when `Main` runs?
options: Startup fails with a circular-dependency exception, because both use constructor injection

Payment successful
Order Details
Order placed

Order placed
Payment successful
Order Details

Payment successful
Order placed, then a `NullPointerException` because `orderService` is still null
questions.explanation: `@Lazy` on the constructor parameter makes Spring inject a proxy, so `OrderService` can be created without a real `PaymentService`, breaking the loop. On the first `pay()` call the proxy creates the real `PaymentService`, injecting the already-existing `OrderService`, so it prints "Payment successful", then "Order Details", and finally `placeOrder()` prints "Order placed". The notes stress this is a workaround - refactoring is the real fix.
questions.source: code: BeanInitializationDemo/OrderService.java, PaymentService.java, Main.java; notes p28-29

questions.question: `OrderService` and `PaymentService` reference each other through `@Autowired` fields. In a plain Spring Core demo this started fine, but the same classes in a Spring Boot 3 app fail at startup with a circular-reference error. What is going on, and what is the best fix?
options: Field injection is not supported in Spring Boot; switch both to setter injection
Spring Boot creates beans in parallel, so the early reference is lost; add `@Order` to both classes
Spring Core could resolve it with an early reference, but Spring Boot (2.6+) prohibits circular references by default; the best fix is to refactor, e.g. move the shared logic into a third bean
Boot needs `spring.main.allow-circular-references=true`, which is the recommended production setting
questions.explanation: With field/setter injection, Spring Core can create one object, expose an early (not yet fully initialized) reference, and finish the other. Spring Boot 2.6+ disables this by default (`spring.main.allow-circular-references=false`). Setting it to `true` is only a workaround; the design smell - two classes knowing too much about each other - is fixed by refactoring, as the lecture's `CircularDependencyDemo` does by removing `PaymentService`'s call back into `OrderService`.

questions.question: `EmailService` is a normal `@Component` (NOT marked `@Lazy`). `UserService` is also a normal `@Component` with constructor `UserService(@Lazy EmailService emailService)`. When is the real `EmailService` object created?
options: Only when `userService.registerUser()` first calls a method on it
Never - `UserService` only ever talks to the proxy
Only when someone calls `context.getBean(EmailService.class)`
During startup anyway, because `EmailService` is itself an eager singleton; `@Lazy` on the parameter only gives `UserService` a proxy
questions.explanation: `@Lazy` on an injection point changes what is injected (a proxy that resolves the target later); it does not change the target bean's own definition. Since `EmailService` is an eager singleton, the container still pre-instantiates it at startup, and the proxy later delegates to that same object. Delaying creation until first use needs `@Lazy` on the class as well, as in the practice question.
questions.source: notes p25-26; practice Q5-Q6, revision C
